opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the progress we've seen comes from a few things converging at the same time.

The biggest driver is foundation models. For a long time robotics was stuck because every task needed its own carefully engineered pipeline: perception, planning and control, each built separately and brittle when anything changed. Large language models and vision-language models gave robots something they never had before, a kind of common sense about the world. A robot can now understand an instruction like "clean up the spill" and reason about what objects are involved, without someone hand-coding every concept. When you extend those models to output actions, the vision-language-action models, you start getting real generalization across tasks, objects and environments.

The second factor is data. Robotics has always had a data problem. You can't scrape the internet for robot actions the way you scrape it for text. But over the past year or two the community got much better at collecting data at scale. That includes teleoperation fleets, cross-embodiment datasets where many labs pool data from different robots, and much better use of simulation. Sim-to-real transfer, which I've worked on for a long time, has matured a lot. For locomotion especially, you can train in simulation with massive parallelism and deploy the policy almost directly on hardware. That's a big reason legged robots and humanoids suddenly look so agile.

The third factor is hardware and money. Actuators, batteries and sensors got cheaper and better, partly thanks to the EV supply chain. And capital poured into the field, so there are now many more talented people and companies working on these problems than five years ago. More shots on goal means faster progress.

I'd add a note of caution, though. The demos are impressive, but there's still a big gap between a great demo and a robot that works reliably for thousands of hours in a messy home or factory. Dexterous manipulation, long-horizon tasks and robustness are still hard. So I'd say we've hit an inflection point in capability, and the next challenge is turning that into reliability and real deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that several things that had been maturing separately for years finally converged, and once they did, progress compounded very quickly.

The first piece is foundation models. For a long time, the bottleneck in robotics wasn't the hardware or even the control algorithms, it was common sense. A robot could walk or grasp, but it had no idea what a kitchen was, or that a cup of water shouldn't be tipped over. Large language and vision-language models gave us that semantic understanding essentially for free. Suddenly a robot could look at a scene, understand an instruction in plain language, and reason about what to do before it ever moved. That changed the whole architecture of how we build these systems.

The second piece is simulation and learning. In my own work, we spent years on sim-to-real transfer for legged locomotion. Training in simulation lets you run millions of trials in hours, and the gap between simulation and the physical world has narrowed enough that policies trained entirely in sim now walk, run, and recover from falls on real hardware. Those techniques have now spread from locomotion into manipulation, which is a much harder problem because contact is so messy.

The third piece is data. The field finally started treating robot data the way the language community treats text: collect a lot of it, across many embodiments and tasks, and train a single model on all of it. Efforts to pool demonstrations across labs and companies showed that a policy trained on diverse data generalizes far better than one trained narrowly. That's the beginning of a flywheel. More deployed robots mean more data, which means better models, which justifies deploying more robots.

And then there's hardware. Humanoids and dexterous hands became much cheaper and more reliable, partly riding on the supply chains built for electric vehicles and drones. When a capable platform drops from hundreds of thousands of dollars to tens of thousands, many more teams can experiment, and the pace of iteration picks up.

I'd add one caution, though. A lot of what you see in demos is still far from robust, general deployment. Success rates in controlled settings don't yet translate to the long tail of real homes and factories. So the progress is genuine and the trajectory is steep, but I think we're at the start of the curve rather than near the end of it.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s the convergence of several things. First, we’ve made a lot of progress in AI, especially in models that can understand language and visual information. That gives robots a better foundation for interpreting what people want and what’s happening around them.

Second, we’re getting better at learning through simulation. A robot can practice a skill across many simulated environments, and then we can transfer what it learns to the physical robot. That makes experimentation much faster.

And third, hardware is improving, which lets more people build systems, collect data, and test ideas. Those advances reinforce each other.

But I’d distinguish an impressive demonstration from a robot that works reliably every day. The progress is exciting, but robustness—handling unexpected situations without someone stepping in—is still a major challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think several things are coming together. First, we’re getting better at training robots in simulation. A robot can practice across many different situations, and then we can transfer what it learns to the real world. That makes the learning process much faster.

Second, advances in AI are giving robots better ways to understand their surroundings and interpret what people want them to do. And the hardware keeps improving, so we can actually test these ideas on capable machines.

But I would distinguish an impressive demonstration from a robot that works reliably every day. The progress is exciting, but handling unexpected situations safely and consistently is still a major challenge.
